heroIntro: Operating a commercial enterprise, manufacturing facility, or service company in Bangladesh requires navigating the rigorous compliance regime of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 (VAT Act 2012). During routine audits, intelligence investigations, or desk reviews, VAT Commissionerates frequently serve registered taxpayers with aggressive audit observations and show-cause notices under Section 73, alleging input tax credit disallowances, unrecorded turnover, or shortfall in withholding VAT (VDS). Unchallenged show-cause notices culminate in unilateral final demand orders, accompanied by coercive bank account attachments under Section 83. Understanding the statutory hierarchy of appeals—from the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 121 to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal under Section 122 and the High Court Division under Article 102—is essential to shield corporate balance sheets.

quickAnswer.title: How Can a Business Defend Against a VAT Audit Demand Notice in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: When served with an audit observation or show-cause notice under Section 73 of the VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012, a business must submit a comprehensive legal and reconciliation reply within the statutory timeline (typically 15 to 30 days) supported by Mushak invoices, purchase ledgers (Mushak 9.1), and bank statements. If an adverse adjudication order is passed, the taxpayer must file a statutory appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 121 within 90 days, depositing 10% of the disputed tax. Adverse appellate decisions can be appealed before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal under Section 122 upon depositing an additional 10%. If authorities freeze company bank accounts without due process, the business can immediately seek a stay order from the High Court Division under Article 102 writ jurisdiction.
highlights: Failure to reply to Section 73 show-cause notices results in ex-parte demand confirmations.
Statutory appeal under Section 121 requires a 10% pre-deposit of the disputed tax amount.
The Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal serves as the final fact-finding judicial forum.
Unlawful bank account freezes can be challenged and stayed via High Court Article 102 writs.

Appellate Hierarchy: Adjudication Officer -> Commissioner (Appeals) -> Appellate Tribunal -> High Court Division.

sections.title: 1. VAT Audit Triggers: How Section 73 Show-Cause Notices Arise
sections.content:
Under the automated VAT online system (IVAS) established pursuant to the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012, registered corporate entities submit monthly returns (Mushak 9.1). Discrepancies between annual audited financial statements, corporate income tax returns submitted to the National Board of Revenue (NBR), and monthly VAT declarations frequently trigger comprehensive audits.

Audits are conducted by the operational Commissionerate audit wings or the central Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID). Common allegations include unrecorded sales turnover, claiming input tax rebates without matching tax invoices (Mushak 6.3), or failing to deduct and deposit Withholding VAT (VDS) under the VAT Deduction at Source Rules 2020.

When discrepancies are flagged, the revenue officer serves a formal show-cause notice under Section 73 of the VAT Act 2012. The notice quantifies an alleged evaded tax amount and summons the taxpayer to explain why the demand, alongside statutory monthly interest of 1% under Section 127 and heavy administrative penalties, should not be confirmed.

sections.title: 2. Technical Defenses: Input Tax Credits, VDS Compliance & Mushak 6.3
sections.content:
A successful defense against a Section 73 notice depends upon structured accounting and statutory reconciliation. Under Section 46 of the VAT Act 2012, a registered supplier is statutorily entitled to claim input tax rebate on goods and services acquired for commercial output, provided tax is documented on a genuine Mushak 6.3 invoice and paid through banking channels.

Audit officers frequently disallow input rebates on technical grounds—such as minor spelling mismatches in the company name, missing treasury chalan numbers, or suppliers failing to upload invoices in the central system. Defense counsel must demonstrate that the taxpayer exercised reasonable commercial diligence and that technical paperwork defects cannot nullify substantive statutory rebate rights.

Similarly, for Withholding VAT (VDS) allegations under Section 49, the defense must compile certified bank transfer slips and VDS certificates (Mushak 6.6) demonstrating that tax was withheld and deposited into the government treasury within the prescribed statutory period, eliminating alleged liability.

sections.title: 3. The Adjudication Hearing: Presenting Books Before the Joint/Deputy Commissioner
sections.content:
Once the written reply is filed, the matter proceeds to an adjudication hearing under Section 73(3) of the Act before the competent revenue authority—typically an Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner, Joint Commissioner, or Commissioner of VAT, depending on the pecuniary threshold of the demand.

The hearing represents the taxpayer's primary opportunity to present original purchase registers (Mushak 6.1), sales registers (Mushak 6.2), commercial bank statements, and audited balances. Specialized tax advocates present oral arguments highlighting that audit teams applied arbitrary gross-profit estimates or incorrectly reclassified exempt items under the First Schedule of the Act.

Following the hearing, the adjudicating officer issues a formal Adjudication Order (Churanto Adesh). If the officer accepts the reconciliation, the proceedings are dropped. However, if the officer confirms the demand, the enterprise has ninety days to seek appellate relief. sections.title: 4. The First Appeal under Section 121: Timelines & The 10% Pre-Deposit Rule
sections.content:
When an unfavorable adjudication order is passed, the taxpayer must not ignore the document. Allowing an adjudication order to become final converts the demand into an undisputed government debt enforceable by coercive distress.

Under Section 121 of the VAT Act 2012, any person aggrieved by an order passed by a revenue officer below the rank of Commissioner may file an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals). The statutory limitation period is ninety (90) days from the date of receipt of the adjudication order. The Commissioner (Appeals) may condone a delay of an additional thirty (30) days upon proof of sufficient cause.

Crucially, Section 121(4) imposes a mandatory financial prerequisite: the appellant must deposit ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount (excluding penalties and interest) at the time of filing the appeal through government treasury chalan. Without proof of this 10% deposit, the memorandum of appeal cannot be admitted for hearing. The Commissioner (Appeals) examines the merits, may stay coercive recovery, and passes an appellate order confirming, altering, or annulling the demand.

sections.title: 5. Second Appeal Before the VAT Appellate Tribunal (Section 122)
sections.content:
If the Commissioner (Appeals) rejects the appeal or confirms an unreasonable demand, the taxpayer's next statutory recourse is the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal (CEVAT) established under Section 122 of the VAT Act 2012. The Appellate Tribunal is a high-level, independent judicial body comprising judicial members (District Judges) and technical members (Customs/VAT Commissioners).

The appeal before the Tribunal must be filed within ninety (90) days of receiving the order from the Commissioner (Appeals) or an order passed directly by a Commissioner. Under Section 122(4), the appellant must deposit an additional ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount, bringing the total pre-deposit to twenty percent (20%).

The Appellate Tribunal operates as the final court of fact. It has statutory authority to examine witness evidence, review complex accounting methodologies, summon books of accounts, and evaluate whether the revenue department acted within the four corners of the statute. Judgments delivered by the Appellate Tribunal establish authoritative precedents for the entire VAT administration.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: VAT Dispute Stages, Pre-Deposits & Fora
sections.content:
The statutory appeal stages, financial deposit mandates, and appellate venues are synthesized in the following comparative matrix:

Dispute Level Adjudicating / Appellate Authority Pre-Deposit Requirement Filing Limitation Period
Primary Adjudication Assistant / Deputy / Joint Commissioner (Sec 73) Nil (Written reply to show-cause) 15 to 30 days from notice service
First Statutory Appeal Commissioner of VAT (Appeals) (Sec 121) 10% of disputed tax amount 90 days (+30 days condonation)
Second Statutory Appeal Customs, Excise & VAT Appellate Tribunal (Sec 122) Additional 10% (cumulative 20%) 90 days from appellate order
High Court Reference / Writ High Court Division (Sec 125 / Art 102) Nil (Discretionary court security) 90 days for Ref; prompt for Writ

sections.title: 7. Resisting Coercive Recovery: Defending Against Section 83 Bank Freezes
sections.content:
One of the most drastic enforcement mechanisms under the VAT Act 2012 is Section 83 ('Recovery of Government Dues'). If a taxpayer fails to pay a confirmed demand or misses the appeal deadline, the VAT Commissionerate issues direct attachment notices to commercial banks under Section 83(1)(c).

The bank is commanded to immediately freeze all operating accounts, fixed deposits, and credit lines of the company, and transmit the funds directly to the NBR treasury. A bank freeze completely paralyzes payroll, vendor payments, and export-import operations. Furthermore, under Section 83(1)(d), officers may padlock commercial premises or seize factory stock.

However, coercive recovery under Section 83 cannot be initiated while an appeal is actively pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal, provided the mandatory pre-deposit was made. If revenue officers issue premature attachment notices in violation of statutory stay principles, emergency legal remedies must be activated immediately.

sections.title: 8. High Court Division Reference Applications & Constitutional Writs (Article 102)
sections.content:
When the statutory tribunal process is exhausted or bypassed due to administrative illegality, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh provides decisive judicial protection.

Under Section 125 of the VAT Act 2012, an aggrieved taxpayer or the Commissioner may file a Reference Application before the High Court Division within ninety days on any question of law arising out of the order of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court evaluates whether the Tribunal misinterpreted statutory definitions or misapplied tax rates.

Concurrently, where revenue officers freeze bank accounts without serving the underlying adjudication order, demand extortionate pre-deposits, or act with mala fides, the company can petition the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution for a Writ of Mandamus or Certiorari. The High Court routinely stays illegal bank freezes, directs unfreezing of commercial accounts, and commands the department to hear appeals on their legal merits. For broader corporate litigation strategies, explore our guide on company and corporate legal services.

sections.title: 9. Illustrative Scenario: Overturning an Arbitrary 5 Crore BDT VAT Demand
sections.content:
To illustrate how technical VAT defense operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A consumer goods manufacturing company in Gazipur received a show-cause notice under Section 73 from the Dhaka North VAT Commissionerate claiming a tax shortfall of 5 Crore BDT plus 2.5 Crore BDT in penalties. The audit team alleged that the enterprise claimed unverified input tax rebates over a 24-month period and failed to deposit VDS on advertising expenditures.

The company engaged a Supreme Court tax advocate. The legal team audited the transaction history, compiled every original Mushak 6.3 invoice, cross-referenced bank clearing slips, and demonstrated that 98% of suppliers had properly recorded transactions in the central IVAS system. Despite this reconciliation, the Deputy Commissioner confirmed the demand ex-parte.

The advocate immediately filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 121, depositing the statutory 10% chalan. When the Commissionerate attempted to freeze the company's operating bank accounts under Section 83 during the appeal pendency, the advocate filed an emergency Writ Petition before the High Court Division. The High Court stayed the bank attachment, reprimanded the department for coercive measures during active appeal, and directed the Commissioner (Appeals) to conduct a full evidentiary review. The appellate authority subsequently vacated 92% of the disputed demand, saving the enterprise from insolvency.

faqs.question: What is a Section 73 show-cause notice under the VAT Act 2012?
faqs.answer: A Section 73 notice is an official legal demand issued by a VAT revenue officer alleging non-payment, short-payment, or irregular rebate of VAT, requiring the taxpayer to show cause why the demanded tax and penalties should not be confirmed.

faqs.question: How long do I have to reply to a VAT show-cause notice in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: The show-cause notice typically stipulates a deadline of 15 to 30 days. It is critical to request an extension if additional time is needed to reconcile accounting ledgers and retrieve Mushak 6.3 invoices.

faqs.question: What is the pre-deposit requirement to file a first VAT appeal?
faqs.answer: Under Section 121(4) of the VAT Act 2012, the appellant must deposit ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount (excluding penalties and interest) through government treasury chalan to have the appeal admitted.

faqs.question: What is the role of the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal?
faqs.answer: The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 122 serves as the final independent statutory court of fact, reviewing complex accounting, legal interpretations, and procedural errors committed by subordinate revenue officers.

faqs.question: Can VAT officers freeze my company's bank accounts under Section 83?
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 83 empowers authorities to attach commercial bank accounts for unpaid government dues. However, freezing accounts while an appeal is actively pending with statutory pre-deposit is illegal and can be stayed by the High Court.

faqs.question: How can the High Court Division intervene in a VAT dispute in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: The High Court Division hears Reference Applications on questions of law under Section 125, and issues Writ Petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution to stay unlawful bank account attachments, arbitrary seizures, or violations of natural justice.

faqs.question: What evidence is required to prove a valid input tax rebate in a VAT audit?
faqs.answer: You must produce valid tax invoices (Mushak 6.3), entries in the purchase register (Mushak 6.1), proof of payment via recognized banking channels, and matching records in the monthly Mushak 9.1 return.

faqs.question: Can a foreign company operating in Bangladesh challenge VAT audit assessments?
faqs.answer: Yes. Foreign branches, liaison offices, and joint-venture companies enjoy identical statutory rights to challenge audit observations, file appeals before the Tribunal, and seek constitutional writ protection before the Supreme Court.
